Expectation1: Maintain regular communication with family members
Situation1: A family member has a new job and has shared some initial excitement about it with their relatives.
Expectation2: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation2: A friend sends a text message complaining about having a long, boring day.
Story:
My phone buzzed twice in quick succession. First, a message from my granddaughter, who had just started her new job. She wrote, “Grandma, I had the best day! I can’t wait to tell you all about it.” I knew how much it meant to her that I listened and celebrated her milestones. My daughter had reminded me just last week, “Mom, she really values your encouragement.” I felt the weight of being the supportive grandmother, the one who always responds quickly and with warmth.

Almost immediately after, my friend Linda texted, “Rough day. Everything felt pointless. Can I talk?” I could almost hear the exhaustion in her words. Linda had been there for me through so much, and I knew she needed someone to listen, not just a quick reply. She expected me to be present, to offer comfort and understanding.

I stared at my phone, feeling the pressure of both roles. My heart tugged in two directions—toward my granddaughter’s joy and Linda’s need for comfort. I wanted to be there for both, but I only had a moment to choose which message to answer first. My fingers hovered over the screen, torn between the expectations of family and friendship.
